components.source_comparison: General definition; the source (pp. 214-215) uses kernels only through mu(omega, A) on Omega x S-sigma-algebra; the entry supplies measurability in the parameter, the probability-measure section and the set-valued second argument. No source variant in the extent is lost.

Durrett p. 214: definition (i)/(ii) with (ii) only for a.e. omega and the regular conditional probability case S = Omega, X identity are on the route (def:p15-regular-conditional-law lines 31-53; def:p15-w02b-p15-008-rcd lines 31-49, with the exceptional-set convention lines 51-60). The p. 214 non-existence remark is reduced to a bare report; its historical attribution and its explanation are absent.
components.gap: Preserve the source's non-existence account (Durrett p. 214) and work the entry's boundary. On the reader route only the bare report survives: 'The source records that regular conditional distributions do not always exist' (conditioning-independence-and-information-w02b-p15-008.tex lines 235-237). Absent from the route are the source's attribution of the first example to Dieudonne (1948), with Doob (1953), p. 624, and Faden (1985) for later developments, and the source's explanation of the difficulty: for disjoint A_1, A_2, ... the identity P(X in U_n A_n | G) = sum_n P(X in A_n | G) holds only almost surely, by (4.1.1) and (4.1.3), so that when S contains enough countable collections of disjoint sets the exceptional null sets pile up. The entry's own boundary claim (regular-conditional-laws.tex lines 49-51) that the special case S = Omega, S-sigma-algebra = F_0, X the identity needs an existence hypothesis on the outcome space is neither demonstrated nor supported on the route beyond that bare report. Text on this exists only in files that are not on the reader route (probability-spaces-and-random-variables-w02c-p15-002.tex lines 726-783; conditioning-independence-and-information-w02c-p15-008.tex lines 1-255) and is not credited here.

components.source_comparison: Durrett p. 214, Theorem 4.1.16 (E|f(X)| finite; indicator, simple, monotone, f+ - f- route): supplied for everywhere-defined kernels and, in the source's almost-everywhere regime, by thm:p15-w02b-p15-008-ae-integration with a written annex proof following the source's route. The source's remark that such laws compute all conditional expectations at once is reflected at lines 4-6 and in the single-kernel formula.

Durrett p. 215, real construction inside Theorem 4.1.17 (rational versions, Omega_o, F(x, omega) = inf G(q, omega), CDF, version identity, Stieltjes measure, pi-lambda): every step written, including the endpoint limits the source leaves to Theorem 3.2.12, a G-measurable good set, a default off it, and uniqueness.

Durrett p. 215, Theorem 4.1.17 'r.c.d.'s exist if (S, S) is nice' with the proof's restatement of nice (one-to-one phi into R, phi and phi^{-1} measurable). The route proves a Borel-image version with full steps, but the source's printed hypothesis and its relation to the Borel-image hypothesis are not supplied.
components.gap: Preserve the source's hypothesis of Theorem 4.1.17 (Durrett p. 215): (S, S-sigma-algebra) nice, which the source's proof restates as a one-to-one map phi: S -> R with phi and phi^{-1} measurable, with no clause requiring phi(S) to be Borel. The route states and proves the theorem only for a measurable isomorphism onto a Borel set E (regular-conditional-laws.tex lines 95-110, annex lines 139-181) and calls this 'the source's standard Borel case with its image and concentration requirements explicit'. It does not state the source's hypothesis in the source's terms, does not establish how it relates to the Borel-image hypothesis (the source's step phi(A) = (phi^{-1})^{-1}(A) in R for every A in S-sigma-algebra, used to set mu(omega, A) = nu(omega, phi(A)), holds exactly when phi(S) is Borel), and does not settle the theorem for nice spaces whose image is not Borel. The routed coding definition (countable-product-measures.tex lines 174-180) likewise identifies the source's nice class with Borel-image codings without stating the source's definition. Text on this exists only in files not on the reader route (probability-spaces-and-random-variables-w02c-p15-002.tex lines 626-658 and 784-874; measure-integration-and-product-constructions-w02c-p15-004.tex from line 254) and is not credited here.

components.source_comparison: Durrett p. 214, continuation of Example 4.1.6 (joint density f > 0, mu(y, A) = int_A f dx / int f dx, r.c.d. for X given sigma(Y)): the route's theorem assumes only f >= 0, normalizes on D = {0 < m < infinity} with a point-mass default, and therefore includes the source's case; proof written; the link to the source's continuation is stated at w02b-p15-008 lines 371-374.

Durrett p. 215, Theorem 4.1.18 (X, Y in a nice space, G = sigma(Y), mu: S x S-sigma-algebra -> [0,1], (i) versions, (ii) a.e. probability measure): the route proves a stronger statement (arbitrary observation space, a measure at every argument, joint formula, uniqueness) for X in a Borel-image coded space; the source's printed nice hypothesis is not supplied.
components.gap: Preserve the source's hypothesis of Theorem 4.1.18 (Durrett p. 215): X and Y take values in a nice space (S, S-sigma-algebra) in the source's printed sense (a one-to-one phi: S -> R with phi and phi^{-1} measurable, no clause requiring phi(S) to be Borel), G = sigma(Y). The route proves the theorem for X in a standard Borel space, i.e. one with a Borel-image coding (regular-conditional-laws.tex lines 133-153, annex lines 183-242), and asserts that 'the source's Theorem 4.1.18, with both variables in the same standard Borel space, is included', without stating the source's hypothesis in its terms, establishing its relation to the Borel-image hypothesis (the transport step mu(y, A) = nu(y, phi(A)) needs phi(A) Borel for every A, which holds exactly when phi(S) is Borel), or settling the theorem for nice spaces whose image is not Borel. Text on this exists only in a file not on the reader route (probability-spaces-and-random-variables-w02c-p15-002.tex lines 784-874) and is not credited here.

components.source_comparison: General construction, no separate source statement in the extent; measurability of sections, countable additivity, uniqueness, nonnegative and signed integration formula and the identification with the joint law of (Y, X) are all written.

Durrett p. 216, Exercise 4.1.4 (p, q in (1, infinity), 1/p + 1/q = 1, conditional Hoelder from the unconditional one via a regular conditional object): statement matches; the integrability hypotheses are those implicit in the source's definition of E(X|F) for E|X| finite (p. 205); proof written via the regular conditional law of the pair.

Durrett p. 210, Example 4.1.8 set-up: uniform point on the globe, longitude in [0, 2 pi), latitude in (-pi/2, pi/2], alternative ranges [0, pi) and (-pi, pi] describing the great circle and the angle on it: supplied with the explicit reparametrization.

Durrett p. 210, Example 4.1.8 'Borel's paradox': the calculation, the independence in both formulations and the nonuniform conditional angle law are on the route with written proofs (and the added Y/(1+X) null-event example is complete); the example's name, the apparent paradox and the source's resolution as its explanation are not.
components.gap: Preserve the source's Example 4.1.8 (Durrett p. 210) as the source presents it: its name, Borel's paradox; the apparent paradox that, for a point chosen uniformly on the globe, both the new longitude theta in [0, pi), which specifies the great circle, and the angle phi in (-pi, pi] along that circle might be expected to be uniform, while theta is uniform and phi is not; and the source's resolution as its explanation: in the new as in the traditional formulation phi is independent of theta, so the conditional distribution is the unconditional one, which is not uniform because more of the surface lies near the equator than near the North Pole. The route (regular-conditional-laws.tex lines 192-248, annex lines 346-389) supplies the two coordinate systems, the independence and the densities 1/(2 pi), cos(phi)/2, 1/pi and |cos psi|/4 with the nonuniform conditional angle law, but neither the name, nor the paradox, nor the resolution as the source's explanation. Text on this exists only in a file not on the reader route (probability-spaces-and-random-variables-w02c-p15-002.tex lines 659-725) and is not credited here.

defect_observations: conditioning-independence-and-information-w02b-p15-008.tex lines 144-149 say that thm:p15-real-conditional-law and thm:p15-standard-conditional-law cover the source's Theorems 4.1.17 and 4.1.18; the handbook form of Theorem 4.1.18 is thm:p15-value-conditional-law, which that sentence does not cite.

regular-conditional-laws.tex lines 187-189 say the proof uses the regular conditional law of the pair 'as requested in the source's Exercise 4.1.4'; the source asks to use a regular conditional probability, which in its own terms (p. 214) is the case S = Omega with X the identity. The substitution, which avoids an existence hypothesis on Omega, is not remarked.

countable-product-measures.tex lines 178-180 say the source calls the class in its Theorem 2.1.22 nice; the source defines nice by the one-to-one-map condition (p. 53) and Theorem 2.1.22 shows that Borel subsets of complete separable metric spaces are nice (bears on the C005 and C007 gaps; another unit's file).

The source's continuation of Example 4.1.6 assumes f(x, y) > 0; the route's theorem drops this (f >= 0, D = {0 < m < infinity}) and includes the source's case, but does not mention the source's positivity hypothesis or that the source's formula is undefined where m = infinity (not verdict-changing).
